reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Suchy Liver Disease in Children
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive cholestatic cirrhosis described in Ojibway-Cree children of northwestern Quebec, caused by a founder mutation in CIRH1A (now UTP4), encoding cirhin
Typically presents with transient neonatal jaundice that resolves, followed by insidious progression to biliary cirrhosis during childhood
Portal hypertension with splenomegaly and oesophageal varices is a common mode of later presentation
Liver biochemistry shows a cholestatic picture, and biopsy demonstrates portal fibrosis progressing to established cirrhosis with bile duct proliferation
Cirhin is a nucleolar protein involved in ribosomal RNA processing; how its dysfunction produces a liver-specific phenotype is not fully understood
A single homozygous founder variant (R565W) accounts for essentially all affected individuals in the original population
Management is supportive with ursodeoxycholic acid and fat-soluble vitamins, and liver transplantation is the definitive treatment for end-stage disease
reference.pathophysiology: North American Indian childhood cirrhosis is an autosomal recessive cholestatic disease caused by a founder missense mutation in CIRH1A (UTP4), which encodes cirhin, a nucleolar protein implicated in pre-ribosomal RNA processing. Affected children develop neonatal cholestasis that appears to remit, but progressive portal and periportal fibrosis continues silently, culminating in biliary cirrhosis and portal hypertension in childhood or adolescence. The exact mechanism by which impaired cirhin function selectively injures the liver remains uncertain, though disturbed ribosome biogenesis and biliary epithelial dysfunction are proposed.
additionalInvestigations: Liver function tests and serum bile acids showing a cholestatic pattern
Abdominal ultrasound and elastography to assess liver architecture and fibrosis
Liver biopsy demonstrating portal fibrosis, ductular reaction, and evolving cirrhosis
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to screen for varices in portal hypertension
Targeted genetic testing for the CIRH1A/UTP4 founder variant
Fat-soluble vitamin levels and coagulation profile
redFlags: Variceal haemorrhage or other complications of portal hypertension
Progressive jaundice and synthetic failure indicating decompensated cirrhosis
Growth failure with severe fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
Ascites or hepatic encephalopathy signalling end-stage liver disease
reference.prognosis: Without treatment the disease progresses to cirrhosis and portal hypertension during childhood or adolescence, and many patients ultimately require liver transplantation, which is curative; outcomes after transplantation are generally good.
pitfalls: Being reassured by the apparent resolution of neonatal jaundice while fibrosis progresses silently
Failing to consider the diagnosis outside a recognised ancestry when the phenotype fits
Delaying variceal surveillance in a child with unexplained splenomegaly
Confusing the histology with biliary atresia or other paediatric cholestatic disorders
